name: Pretraining
summary: Training a model from scratch on huge amounts of text by asking it, over and over, to predict the next token and correcting its mistakes.

D1.guide: Try it: cover the next word in a sentence and guess it.
text: Imagine reading millions of books where the next word is always covered. You guess, peek, and learn a tiny bit from every wrong guess.
Do that trillions of times and you become very good at guessing. That's pretraining.
D1.analogy: Guess the covered word, then peek.

text: The training objective is simple: for each position in a batch of text, predict the next token. The difference between the prediction and the real token is the **loss**.
**Gradient descent** nudges every weight slightly to reduce that loss, batch after batch, on large GPU clusters.
Loss tends to fall predictably as models, data and compute grow together (**scaling laws**). The result is a **base model** that continues text but doesn't yet follow instructions.
D2.analogy: Guess the covered word, then peek.
D2.analogyBreaks: A reader understands the story while guessing. The model only adjusts numbers to make the right token more likely; abilities like arithmetic or translation emerge unevenly from that single objective.

predict.question: You type a question into a freshly pretrained base model. What does it usually do?
options: Continues the text, perhaps with more questions or an unrelated paragraph
predict.explanation: A base model has only learned to continue text; following instructions comes from post-training.

text: Open questions: how much more high-quality data exists, the balance between model size and training tokens (compute-optimal scaling), whether some abilities emerge suddenly or only look sudden, and how much synthetic data can substitute for human text.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
